prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated-insulator and superconducting states, opening the field of moire quantum matter.

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots I still put B001 first. It has the most first-place rankings (four of eight, with a fifth member at rank 2), but I rest the case on the science, not the count. A concrete, falsifiable prediction (Bistritzer-MacDonald flat bands at a magic angle) was followed years later by an experiment that found correlated insulators and superconductivity near that angle, and the result has been reproduced by many independent groups in twisted bilayer graphene, twisted multilayers and twisted TMDs. A theorist can respect a case where the clue was found in nature, because the prediction was tested rather than only elegant. The theory-plus-experiment split across three names is natural and fits the prize limit. Eight years is a mature, not premature, interval, because the existence of flat-band correlated phases does not depend on the pairing mechanism.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the physics is still moving. The superconducting mechanism is unresolved, device-to-device and twist-angle variability complicate several states, and a committee that wants a settled interpretation could reasonably wait. Attribution is also hard: the Cao first-author role, the Fatemi, Dean, Efetov, Young and Yazdani groups, and earlier twisted-graphene theory all have claims that three names cannot honour. The experimental half of the discovery is spread over several laboratories while the prize would name one experimental leader.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B001 only fourth because confirmation is broad but the superconducting mechanism is unsettled, so recognition may be somewhat early and the committee might wait for a stable interpretation.
responses.response: I take the point about the mechanism, but I do not think the criterion is a settled microscopic theory of the superconductor. The discovery is that flat bands at the predicted angle produce correlated insulators and superconductivity, and that is robust across many groups. Prizes have repeatedly honoured discoveries whose full explanation came later. I do agree with Kroll that this raises the bar for the citation wording, which should credit the prediction and the discovery of the phases and not claim an explanation of the pairing.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the Katori-Ye optical lattice clock first as a clean, original invention with extensive independent confirmation and ripe timing because of the redefinition of the second, and ranks B001 fourth because its interpretation is not fully stable.
responses.response: B007 is a strong and cleaner two-person case, and that is why it is my first alternative. Where I differ is that the clock refines a measurement field already honoured by the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion prize, whereas twisted bilayer graphene opened a new class of tunable correlated matter. I also doubt that unresolved interpretation counts more heavily against B001 than the pending SI redefinition counts against B007's formal impact. I would not object to B007 as the next prize, but I think B001 has more scientific novelty now.

responses.point: Mehlig supports B001 first but proposes only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, calling the two-person version cleanest while noting that it leaves out Bistritzer.
responses.response: I disagree with dropping Bistritzer. The 2011 paper is a two-author prediction, and the magic-angle flat-band calculation is exactly the quantitative claim that was later tested. Leaving out its first author to make the prize look tidier would be an attribution error, and the three-name limit lets us avoid it. The cost is that the experimental side has a single name, and I would rather accept that imbalance openly than shrink the theory credit.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the aberration-corrected electron optics candidate B030 first on the strength of a clear invention that transformed materials imaging, while acknowledging that Krivanek's competing claim is not in the credited names.
responses.response: I agree that B030 is a real invention with huge practical impact, and mature by any standard. My concern is the one Olsson raises herself: with Krivanek missing from the credited names, the TEM/STEM split leaves the attribution open, and no one else on the committee ranked it. I would not place it in the preferred configuration, although I accept that it would be a defensible instrumentation prize on its own merits.

uncertainties: Whether the experimental credit should rest on Jarillo-Herrero alone or whether Cao, Fatemi or other groups (Dean, Efetov, Young, Yazdani) require a different allocation than the supplied names allow.
Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism makes the committee prefer to wait, which depends on how it weights stability of interpretation against a clearly reproduced phenomenon.
Whether B007 should be preferred this year on cleanliness of attribution alone, given that B001 has more first-place support but a harder credit allocation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001, B007 or B023. My documented connections are my PhD supervisor David Gross, my early mentor Hector Rubinstein, my co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group, and none is a credited name here. My own work is in string theory and cosmology, not condensed matter, so I judge the condensed-matter cases as an outsider relying on colleagues' expertise.
